Java.basis: language-level dependency semantics: JDK self-sufficiency for compile/run, JPMS module declarations vs classic classpath ambiguity risk
raw_observations: Java core language plus JDK (javac/java) has zero external native dependencies to build or run a program: 'javac Main.java && java Main' works with only the JDK installed.
Reviewed /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/java/micro and /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/java/adversarial: sample programs compile and run using only javac/java, no third-party jars required.

Transitive dependency resolution is delegated to external build tools (Maven/Gradle), not part of the core language; keeps runtime dependency-free but pushes complexity to tooling for larger projects.
Module system (JPMS, Java 9+) allows explicit dependency declaration via module-info.java, improving clarity over classic classpath model, but ecosystem adoption is inconsistent.
Classic classpath model can allow ambiguous or duplicate class resolution across jars (classpath hell); JPMS mitigates but does not eliminate this broadly.
Java.score_rationale: Java core language and JDK have a minimal build/run dependency surface, scoring well on dependency simplicity intrinsic to the language. Not 100 because reliance on classpath-based transitive resolution outside JPMS modules, and historical classpath ambiguity, are language/runtime-model properties adding non-trivial complexity relative to languages with simpler, more explicit dependency models.

Java.basis: language/runtime design: bytecode abstraction, standard library cross-platform APIs, opt-in native interop boundary
raw_observations: Java's language/runtime design (JVM bytecode target, write-once-run-anywhere) is intrinsically platform-neutral by construction: source compiles to platform-independent bytecode executed by any conformant JVM.

No platform-specific conditional compilation is required in the base language for portability; standard library APIs (java.nio.file, java.net) provide cross-platform abstractions such as Path and separator handling.

Reviewed /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/java/micro and adversarial samples: no platform-specific code, OS-conditional branches, or native-only APIs used; portable across JVM-supporting platforms by design.

Native interop (JNI/JNA/Foreign Function and Memory API) is opt-in and clearly separated from the portable core language, preserving platform neutrality of the base language while still allowing platform-specific extension when needed.

Design-level caveat: some JDK APIs and behaviors have historically differed slightly between platforms (filesystem case sensitivity, line endings, default charset behavior pre-Java 18), minor language/runtime design leaks rather than ecosystem gaps.
Java.score_rationale: Very high score reflecting the deliberate design goal and structural mechanism (bytecode plus JVM abstraction layer) achieving genuine platform neutrality at the language/runtime level, distinct from breadth of actually-shipped JVM ports (an Ecosystem concern). Slight deduction for minor historically-observed platform-dependent default behaviors baked into standard library design rather than left fully abstracted.
